title: When choice becomes a burden
text: In a famous experiment, a Californian supermarket displayed twenty-four varieties of jam one weekend and {{1}} six the next. Shoppers could taste {{2}} display, yet {{3}} smaller line-up outsold the bigger one by a factor of ten. As the evidence accumulated, retailers realised that {{4}} much choice can paralyse: too many options invite regret, comparison and delay, and the shopper who came for toothpaste leaves with {{5}}. {{6}} is easier to choose from six jars than from sixty, not because six is a magic number {{7}} because a smaller set feels completable — each option can actually be considered. The lesson now shapes everything from restaurant menus to software settings, {{8}} designers increasingly hide complexity behind a gentle, well-chosen default.

gaps.hint: adverb: twenty-four varieties ___ six the next
gaps.explanation: The focusing adverb stresses how few: only six.
'Either display' — one or the other of the two.
The line-up is identified by its comparative: the smaller one.
'Leaves with nothing' — the outcome of paralysis; 'not anything' would be two words.

gaps.hint: dummy subject: ___ is easier to choose
gaps.explanation: 'It is easier to…' — the dummy subject before the infinitive.

gaps.hint: conjunction: not because six is magic ___ because
gaps.explanation: 'Not because … but because' — the fixed pair.

gaps.hint: conjunction: software settings, ___ designers hide complexity
gaps.explanation: The result clause after the comma: so designers hide.
